title: Union Minister Dr. Jitendra Singh Emphasises deeper Integration of Traditional Knowledge with Modern Science and Medicine
subtitle:
Traditional Knowledge Should Move Beyond Conventional Boundaries and Connect with Modern Science, Medicine and Emerging Technologies: Dr. Jitendra Singh
Dr. Jitendra Singh Visits CSIR-TKDL as Traditional Knowledge Repository Expands Beyond Medicinal Formulations
body_text:
Traditional knowledge should not remain confined to conventional systems of medicine but should seek deeper integration with Medicine, modern science and emerging technologies to widen its reach and societal impact, Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science and Technology and Earth Sciences and MoS PMO, Personnel, Public Grievances, Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr Jitendra Singh, said during his visit to the CSIR-"Traditional Knowledge Digital Library" (CSIR-TKDL) here today.
Dr Jitendra Singh emphasised the need for greater outreach and a wider scope of work in the field of traditional knowledge. He said that traditional knowledge should not be viewed only through the prism of Ayurveda and other indigenous systems, but should increasingly be connected with institutions and disciplines across science and medicine as India moves towards a more integrated approach to research and innovation.
The Minister called for stronger collaboration between CSIR-TKDL and academic and medical institutions. He suggested greater scholarly engagement, including opportunities for co-guidance of postgraduate medical students, to expand traditional knowledge research among students and the wider research community. He noted that such collaborations would also help connect the work of TKDL with the younger generation.
Dr. Jitendra Singh also underlined the importance of bringing together cutting-edge technology and India's rich repository of traditional knowledge. He observed that India's advanced scientific and technological capabilities, together with its extensive traditional knowledge base, provide an opportunity to develop a more integrated approach to research and innovation.
During the interaction, the Minister was briefed on the evolution of TKDL from an initiative focused on digitising traditional knowledge into a structured knowledge resource that makes such knowledge accessible and understandable in modern scientific and intellectual property terminology. The initiative was institutionalised in 2001, initially focusing on Ayurveda formulations, and was subsequently expanded to cover other systems of traditional knowledge.
The discussions also highlighted the data architecture and standardised terminology developed for TKDL, enabling effective searches and presentation of traditional knowledge in formats that can be understood by patent examiners. The knowledge resources have been made available to patent offices in multiple languages, including English, French, German, Japanese and Spanish.
The Minister was informed that TKDL has played an important role in preventing the grant of patents based on already documented traditional knowledge. The database has also continued to expand beyond traditional medicinal formulations to cover areas including diagnostic methods, devices and surgical practices.
Dr. Jitendra Singh called for further strengthening the academic and educational outreach of TKDL. He highlighted the need to familiarise younger students and researchers with traditional knowledge, intellectual property and the processes involved in documenting and protecting such knowledge. The interaction also covered ongoing online learning and capacity-building initiatives aimed at widening access to education related to traditional knowledge.
The Minister further emphasised the potential of collaboration between traditional knowledge institutions and organisations working in modern medicine and scientific research. Referring to emerging research and studies involving traditional practices, he stressed the importance of expanding institutional engagement and encouraging evidence-based work that connects traditional knowledge with contemporary scientific approaches.
During the visit, Dr. Jitendra Singh also visited the book stall and digital library, reviewing resources and knowledge collections associated with TKDL. He interacted with officials and experts on the work being undertaken to document, organise and disseminate India's traditional knowledge in a structured digital format.
The Minister also participated in a plantation activity during the visit, reinforcing the broader emphasis on connecting knowledge, science and societal engagement.
The programme was attended by Dr. M. Kalaiselvi, Director General, CSIR and Secretary, DSIR; Dr. Viswajanni Sattigari, Head, CSIR-TKDL; and Shri Mahendra Kumar Gupta, Joint Secretary, CSIR, among other officials and experts.
Dr. Jitendra Singh expressed confidence that CSIR-TKDL, by widening its outreach, strengthening interdisciplinary collaborations and connecting traditional knowledge with contemporary science and technology, can further enhance the relevance and impact of India's rich traditional knowledge repository.

enrichment.summary: Union Minister Dr Jitendra Singh visited CSIR's Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) and called for deeper integration of traditional knowledge with modern science, medicine and emerging technologies, urging collaboration between TKDL and academic/medical institutions. He was briefed on TKDL's evolution since its 2001 institutionalisation from an Ayurveda-focused digitisation project into a structured resource in multiple languages that helps prevent patents on already-documented traditional knowledge, now expanding into diagnostics, devices and surgical practices.
enrichment.context:
TKDL was established in 2001 as a joint initiative of CSIR and the Ministry of AYUSH to codify traditional knowledge (initially Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha and Yoga formulations) into a searchable database using a specially developed classification system, the Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification (TKRC). Its primary purpose is defensive protection against 'biopiracy' — preventing foreign patent offices from granting patents on traditional knowledge that already exists in the public domain in India, a concern that gained prominence after controversies over patents on turmeric, neem and basmati rice in the 1990s. TKDL has since been shared with patent offices in the US, Europe, UK, Germany, Japan and others under access agreements, and has reportedly led to the cancellation or withdrawal of numerous patent applications globally.

This particular release is essentially a report of a ministerial visit and speech, containing no new policy announcement, scheme, or funding decision — the Minister's remarks are aspirational calls for greater academic collaboration and interdisciplinary integration. However, the factual background on TKDL's structure, history and role in IPR protection is examinable, making it moderately useful for aspirants tracking India's traditional knowledge and intellectual property ecosystem.

prelims_questions.question: The 'Traditional Knowledge Digital Library' (TKDL), often in news for preventing biopiracy, is an initiative of which of the following?
options: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and Ministry of AYUSH
Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
prelims_questions.explanation: TKDL was set up jointly by CSIR and the Ministry of AYUSH in 2001 to document traditional knowledge, initially covering Ayurveda formulations, in order to prevent wrongful patenting.

prelims_questions.question: What is the primary objective of the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL)?
options: To commercially license traditional medicine formulations to pharmaceutical companies
To provide financial subsidies to traditional medicine practitioners
To present India's traditional knowledge in a format understandable to patent examiners so as to prevent grant of patents on already-known knowledge
To regulate the export of medicinal plants
prelims_questions.explanation: TKDL was created to translate and structure traditional knowledge using standardised terminology so that patent offices worldwide can access it and avoid granting patents on knowledge that is already documented and in the public domain in India.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) in protecting India's traditional knowledge from biopiracy. What further steps can be taken to integrate traditional knowledge with modern scientific research?
Examine the challenges and opportunities in mainstreaming traditional knowledge systems within India's formal scientific and medical research ecosystem.

study_notes.reason: The release itself is a ministerial visit report with no new policy content, but the background facts about TKDL — its origin, purpose, structure and IPR role — are classic UPSC objective-question material, outweighing the thin analytical content of the Minister's aspirational remarks.

prelims.point: TKDL (Traditional Knowledge Digital Library) was institutionalised in 2001 as a joint initiative involving CSIR, initially focused on digitising Ayurveda formulations, later expanded to other traditional knowledge systems.
prelims.why_important: The founding year and initial scope of TKDL is a classic fact UPSC tests, often alongside its later expansion into Unani, Siddha and Yoga.

prelims.point: TKDL uses a specially developed classification and standardised terminology (Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification) to present traditional knowledge in formats understandable to patent examiners.
prelims.why_important: UPSC frequently tests the mechanism by which TKDL achieves its defensive protection purpose, distinguishing it from a simple digital archive.

prelims.point: TKDL's primary function is defensive protection against biopiracy — preventing patent offices abroad from granting patents on traditional knowledge already documented and in the public domain in India.
prelims.why_important: This is the core rationale for TKDL's existence and a likely factual distractor in questions about India's IPR/biopiracy safeguards.

prelims.point: TKDL knowledge resources have been shared with patent offices in multiple languages including English, French, German, Japanese and Spanish.
prelims.why_important: Tests awareness of the international reach of TKDL's access arrangements with foreign patent offices.

prelims.point: TKDL's scope has expanded beyond medicinal formulations to cover diagnostic methods, devices and surgical practices.
prelims.why_important: Shows the evolving coverage of TKDL, useful for distinguishing its original versus current mandate.

mains.point: The Minister's call for integrating traditional knowledge with mainstream medical and scientific research reflects a broader policy push for evidence-based validation of traditional practices rather than treating them as a separate silo.
mains.theme: Integration of traditional knowledge with modern science
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on how India can leverage traditional knowledge systems for innovation and healthcare while ensuring scientific validation.
